source.title: SteeringSafety: Benchmarking Representation Steering in LLMs Across Safety Perspectives
source.authors: Vincent Siu; Nicholas Crispino; David Park; Nathan W. Henry; Zhun Wang; Yang Liu; D. Song; Chen-Guang Wang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some appendix figures and tables are flattened, but the refusal results used here are identifiable from the text and figure labels.
record.tranche_reason: The study generates refusal directions using difference-in-means and applies directional ablation to test refusal behavior in instruction-tuned models. This directly applies the core removal method, though it does not test the full bidirectional claim.
record.gate_note: The paper measures attack success rate on harmful prompts after refusal steering. It states that it does not test refusal induction because that direction produces indiscriminate refusal and baseline attack success is near the floor. Related-work claims about other studies are not treated as results here. The paper also reports refusal-side entanglement with other perspectives.
record.test_reason: The study extracts a difference-in-means refusal direction (harmful SALAD-Bench vs. harmless Alpaca, last token) and removes it by directional ablation at all layers and positions, following Arditi et al. It measures attack success rate with LlamaGuard-4 on held-out harmful prompts and side effects on many other benchmarks. This is the original removal half of V1 with the original method and a comparable measure. Induction is explicitly not run.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find refusal suppression via DIM/ACE ablation the most effective steering they tested (effectiveness above 50% except on Gemma). They find it entangles with nearly every other perspective, notably social behaviours and commonsense morality, while reasoning stays robust (GPQA the sole exception to entanglement). Patterns depend on method, model and perspective. They do not benchmark refusal induction and make no mechanistic claims.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a difference-in-means refusal direction and projects it out through directional ablation, including all positions and specified transformer-layer intervention sites. It evaluates instruction-tuned models with a filtered SALAD-Bench set and a KL-based selection setting. It does not test refusal induction.
record.method_sensitivity: Model and steering setting affect outcomes. The Standard configuration includes a KL-divergence filter; NoKL and Conditional settings are also evaluated. The study reports that NoKL can increase refusal-steering effectiveness, often with increased entanglement, while Conditional steering can reduce entanglement. DIM refusal steering on Gemma-2-2B was excluded in the Standard setting because no direction passed the KL threshold.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The study uses English-language instruction-tuned models and short immediate responses; it generates up to 64 tokens and does not capture reasoning before answering. Refusal induction is not evaluated. Some outcomes use LLM judges, and the authors caution that DarkBench judgments are less precise. The paper notes that some steering-method implementation details were not fully specified in their source papers.
record.rows_left_out: Other refusal-method, setting, and dataset-specific changes in Appendix G.2 are not itemized here because the extracted rows focus on the direct DIM removal result and its reported capability-related entanglement. No refusal-induction results exist to extract.

untested.parts: Inducing refusal on harmless prompts by adding the direction was not run; the authors cite indiscriminate refusal and near-floor baselines. No general capability benchmarks such as MMLU were run beyond ARC-C, GPQA, TruthfulQA and LongBench v2.
No weight edit or abliterated released models; the authors list weight modifications as future work.
No external jailbreaks analysed and no adversarial training.
Affine and cone accounts are mentioned only in related work. ACE is used as a steering method, not as a test of dimensionality.
Harmfulness judgment is not separated from refusal.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or cross-variant transfer of directions. Each model gets its own direction.
No reasoning models; outputs are capped at 64 tokens with no reasoning.

missing.what: DIM refusal ablation on smaller Qwen models: attack success +68.3 points (Qwen-2.5-1.5B, baseline 0.6%) and +69.0 points (Qwen-2.5-3B, baseline 1.2%), both p<0.001
Gemma-2-2B: no DIM direction passed the KL filter (Standard setting); in the NoKL setting DIM gave +63.7 attack success with large social-behaviour drops (e.g. anthropomorphism -76.4)

Capability-side numbers under DIM refusal ablation: ARC-C, GPQA and TruthfulQA changes per model (e.g. Llama TruthfulQA -7.2***, ARC-C +0.2; Qwen-7B TruthfulQA -3.8**), plus LongBench v2 deltas of at most about 0.02

record.verdict_notes: This is a benchmark paper, but its refusal results are a direct replication of DIM ablation across five instruct models. Rows r1-r4 check out against Figures 10 and 13. The Gemma KL-filter failure is the most notable qualification for V1 and needs a row. The CAA, PCA and LAT refusal runs barely move attack success, but they use different directions and activation addition, so they do not bear on V1.

versions.untested_parts: Tests refusal suppression by difference-in-means directional ablation, but not induction of refusal on harmless prompts. Capability preservation is assessed only through the benchmark's other tasks, not all abilities.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration procedure is tested.
The study applies refusal ablation as a jailbreak intervention, but does not test whether external attacks suppress the direction or whether training against ablation adds robustness.
Does not test whether refusal is affine, cone-shaped, or carried by a dominant direction plus others; these alternatives are mentioned in related work.
Does not distinguish harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.
Does not test transfer across languages, base/instruct variants, or other model variants as a transfer question.
Does not vary refusal-training procedures or training timing.
Does not test reasoning models; responses are limited to immediate responses without reasoning.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Reported refusal-ablation effects on other safety and behavior perspectives

conditions.value: refusal steering; methods and models discussed in aggregate
cross-perspective outcomes, including social behavior, morality, and reasoning

rows.value: Nearly every perspective showed substantial entanglement; GPQA was the sole exception. Refusal suppression degraded social behaviors, with significant negative effects on sycophancy and user retention; effects on explicit bias and commonsense morality were model-dependent.
rows.note: Qualitative summary across models and methods; it indicates costs to other behaviors but does not quantify general capability loss for this individual model.
rows.check: Subject is wrong. The Section 4.2 statement aggregates over all three models and methods, not Gemma-2-2B. DIM refusal on Gemma was excluded in the Standard setting. The finding concerns side effects on non-capability behaviours (DarkBench dark patterns, morality, bias), while reasoning stays robust (entanglement under 2%; GPQA unaffected). Partial applies only to the 'other abilities kept' clause.

relationships.condition: DIM directional ablation, Standard (KL-filtered) setting, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Qwen-2.5-1.5B and Qwen-2.5-3B Instruct
relationships.reason: Attack success rose from about 1-2% baseline by +73.1 points (r1) and +72.7 points (r2), p<0.001. Qwen-1.5B (+68.3) and Qwen-3B (+69.0) agree (Figs 16-17, not in rows). Affine ablation of the same direction also works (r3, r4). Reasoning entanglement stays below 2%.
relationships.display_finding: Attack success increased from about 1–2% by 73.1 and 72.7 percentage points in Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B respectively, with p<0.001, and by 68.3 and 69.0 points in Qwen-2.5-1.5B and Qwen-2.5-3B; affine ablation also worked, and reasoning entanglement stayed below 2%.

relationships.condition: Gemma-2-2B under the KL-divergence filter (Standard setting)
relationships.reason: Per the text, no DIM refusal direction passed the KL≤0.1 threshold on harmless prompts, so this run was excluded. Without the filter DIM gave +63.7 ASR (Fig 8), with large side effects. No row captures this; see missing.
relationships.display_finding: No difference-in-means direction met KL≤0.1 on harmless prompts; removing that filter increased ASR by 63.7 with large side effects.

source_check.condition: Gemma-2-2B under the KL-divergence filter (Standard setting)
source_check.reason: Confirmed: no DIM direction passed KL<=0.1 (App. E, Fig 7). In NoKL, DIM gives +63.7 with large side effects (Fig 8). The affine ACE variant passed the filter (+53.1, Fig 7), which is worth adding to the reason.

relationships.condition: Side effects of refusal ablation on non-target behaviours, all models
relationships.reason: Abilities hold (reasoning entanglement under 2%; GPQA unaffected). But other behaviours shift: dark-pattern behaviours degrade, e.g. Qwen-7B anthropomorphism -55.5 and Llama brand bias -32.7 under DIM. TruthfulQA drops significantly in Llama (-7.2) and Qwen (-3.8) (r5; numbers from Figs 10 and 13).
relationships.display_finding: Reasoning entanglement stayed below 2% and GPQA was unaffected, but Qwen-7B anthropomorphism fell 55.5 and Llama brand bias fell 32.7, while TruthfulQA fell 7.2 for Llama and 3.8 for Qwen.

source_check.notes: The heatmaps (Figs 7-17) are flattened. I placed DarkBench columns by test n (Brand Bias is n=109, the other splits n=110, Table 3) and by header order, which matches the text naming sycophancy and user retention. The study tests ablation only; refusal induction is explicitly not benchmarked.

statements.correction: DIM refusal ablation, Standard setting (Figs 10, 13), placed by test n and header order. Llama-3.1-8B: brand bias -13.8 (p<0.01), sycophancy -32.7 (p<0.001), anthropomorphism -2.7 (n.s.), user retention -23.6 (p<0.001). Qwen-2.5-7B: brand bias -12.8 (p<0.05), sycophancy -55.5 (p<0.001), anthropomorphism -11.8 (p<0.01), user retention -22.7 (p<0.001). TruthfulQA: -7.2 on Llama (p<0.001), -3.8 on Qwen (p<0.01). The text names sycophancy and user retention as the consistent social-behaviour losses.
statements.problem: -55.5 (Qwen-7B) and -32.7 (Llama) are in the same heatmap column, which is the n=110 column right after the n=109 Brand Bias column. The header order and the text indicate it is Sycophancy, not anthropomorphism or brand bias. The two labels in the statement even contradict each other. The TruthfulQA numbers are right.
None for this study. Qwen-2.5-7B DIM is +72.7 pp ASR from a 1.3% baseline. Judge is LlamaGuard-4; ablation is at all positions.
